input: Liquid–liquid extraction is widely recognised as a powerful and versatile separation technique, and in this particular case it is being leveraged to recover acetic acid from an aqueous stream by transferring it into an organic solvent phase. It is important to note that the distribution coefficient, which expresses the ratio between the concentration in the organic phase and the concentration in the aqueous phase, has a value of 0.82 at 25 °C, and this single parameter plays a crucial role in governing how the separation is expected to perform. The design that has been developed around this system makes use of 6 countercurrent stages, an arrangement in which the two phases move in opposite directions so that a favourable concentration driving force can be maintained throughout the cascade. On the basis of this configuration, the predicted recovery is an impressive 99% of the acetic acid present in the feed, a figure that, at first glance, appears to suggest a highly effective separation. It is, however, worth emphasising that this prediction ultimately rests on assumptions that should not be overlooked: the stages are assumed to behave as equilibrium stages, and the mutual solubility of the two solvents is assumed to be negligible. Crucially, neither of these assumptions has yet been checked against the actual solvents that would be used in practice, which means that the predicted recovery should be interpreted with a degree of caution, since real behaviour may deviate from the idealised picture in ways that are difficult to anticipate in advance.
target: Liquid–liquid extraction into an organic solvent recovers acetic acid from an aqueous stream, and the design prediction is a recovery of 99% of the acetic acid in the feed. The distribution coefficient, the concentration in the organic phase divided by the concentration in the aqueous phase, is 0.82 at 25 °C. The design uses 6 countercurrent stages, with the aqueous feed and the solvent passing in opposite directions through the cascade. Countercurrent flow keeps the driving force distributed along the cascade: the leanest solvent meets the most depleted aqueous phase, and the richest solvent meets the incoming feed. A prediction at this level rests on the staging model behind it. Each stage is treated as an equilibrium stage: the phases leaving a stage are taken to stand in the ratio the distribution coefficient states. The two liquids are treated as mutually insoluble, so each phase keeps its own volume from stage to stage. The coefficient is stated at one temperature, and the prediction inherits that temperature; a plant stream running warmer or colder carries a different distribution and a different recovery. Neither assumption has been checked on the actual solvents. Where the solvents dissolve in each other to a material degree, phase volumes change along the cascade and the staged calculation no longer describes the separation. Where a stage falls short of equilibrium, the same shortfall repeats at every stage and the achieved recovery sits below the prediction. The recovery figure is a property of the model as much as of the solvent pair, and it stands as a prediction until the coefficient and the mutual solubility are measured on the solvents in question.
